Guide for Evaluators

Source: vignettes/evaluator-guide.Rmd
evaluator-guide.Rmd

Overview

The evaluatr package allows you to independently evaluate a clinical prediction model in your own dataset, without the model developer ever seeing your patient data. This guide walks you through the complete workflow from installation to performance reporting.

The system works as follows. The model developer stores their model specification in a private GitHub repository. You use evaluatr to retrieve those specifications and compute predictions entirely within your own R session. Your patient data never leaves your computer.

Installation 

devtools::install_github("JoieEnsor/evaluatr")
library(evaluatr)

Finding available models

Use list_registered_models() to browse publicly registered models and find the developer contact for requesting access:

models <- list_registered_models()
print(models[, c("model_id", "model_name", "developer_email")])

What the developer will send you

Once a developer has agreed to grant you access, they will send you four pieces of information:

  1. Their GitHub username — identifies the account hosting the model
  2. The repository name — the name of the private repository
  3. The model ID — a short identifier matching a folder in the repository (e.g. "dvt_model_v1")
  4. A time-limited access token — a fine-grained GitHub personal access token giving read-only access to their repository

Pass the token directly into the function call as shown in the examples below.

Example 1: Basic whole-dataset evaluation

This example uses the DVT diagnosis dataset included with the package, validated against a logistic regression model hosted on the public evaluatr demo repository. It illustrates the complete evaluatr workflow for a binary outcome model, and you can run it yourself exactly as written — no developer contact required.

library(evaluatr)

# Load the DVT example dataset
dvt_path <- system.file("extdata", "dvt_example.csv", package = "evaluatr")
dvt_data <- read.csv(dvt_path)

# Use studies 6 and 7 as the external validation set
# (studies 1-5 were used for model development)
dvt_val <- dvt_data[dvt_data$study %in% c(6, 7), ]

# Run secure validation against the public evaluatr demo model.
# The token below is a shared public demo credential (not a real GitHub
# token) for demonstration purposes only. In real use, the model developer
# provides you with a private-repo GitHub token.
result <- secure_model_validation(
  repo_owner      = "JoieEnsor",
  repo_name       = "evaluatr-demo-models",
  model_id        = "dvt_logistic_v1",
  github_token    = "evaluatr-demo",
  validation_data = dvt_val,
  outcome         = "dvt"
)

The result object contains a shuffled prediction-outcome matrix. The shuffling means that predictions cannot be matched back to individual patient rows, which ensures the package cannot be used to generate predictions for individual patients in clinical practice.

# Compute performance metrics
performance <- eval_performance(
  validation_result    = result,
  generate_plots       = TRUE,
  confidence_intervals = TRUE,
  n_boot               = 50,      # low here for illustration purposes
  decision_threshold   = 0.15     # set to the clinically relevant threshold
)

# View the metrics table
performance$metrics

# Access individual diagnostic plots
performance$plots$calibration      # calibration plot
performance$plots$decision_curve   # decision curve analysis
performance$plots$distribution     # predicted probability distributions

The metrics table includes the following:

Domain Metrics
Discrimination AUROC / c-statistic
Calibration Intercept, slope, ICI, ECI, ECE, O:E ratio
Overall performance Brier score, Nagelkerke R², Cox-Snell R², McFadden R²
Clinical utility Net benefit, standardised net benefit

Example 2: Subgroup evaluation

Many validation studies assess model performance separately within clinically relevant subgroups, such as sex, age group, or recruitment site. evaluatr supports this through the by argument.

The workflow has two stages. First, pass by to secure_model_validation() so that the subgroup label is retained alongside each shuffled prediction. Second, pass result$shuffled_by to eval_performance() to obtain separate metrics per subgroup.

# Stage 1 — run validation retaining study labels
result_by_study <- secure_model_validation(
  repo_owner      = "developer-username",
  repo_name       = "my-models",
  model_id        = "dvt_v1",
  github_token    = "token_provided_by_developer",
  validation_data = dvt_val,
  outcome         = "dvt",
  by              = "study"     # column name in your dataset
)

# Stage 2 — compute metrics separately per study
performance_by_study <- eval_performance(
  validation_result    = result_by_study,
  generate_plots       = TRUE,
  confidence_intervals = TRUE,
  n_boot               = 50,      # low here for illustration purposes
  decision_threshold   = 0.15,
  by                   = result_by_study$shuffled_by
)

# The metrics table now has a Subgroup column
performance_by_study$metrics

# Plots are organised by subgroup level
performance_by_study$plots[["6"]]$calibration   # study 6
performance_by_study$plots[["7"]]$calibration   # study 7

Each subgroup must contain at least 50 observations. If any subgroup is smaller than this, secure_model_validation() will return an informative error before any predictions are computed.

Example 3: Models requiring pre-processed variables

Some models are developed using transformed or derived variables — for example, an age-squared term or a log-transformed biomarker. How you handle this depends on whether the developer has embedded the transformation in their model specification.

When you need to pre-process (developer specifies transformed variable names)

If the model requires a variable named log_pr (log-progesterone), you will need to create that column in your dataset before calling secure_model_validation(). The developer should document which transformations are required in their publication or access token communication.

bc_path <- system.file("extdata", "bc_survival_example.csv",
                       package = "evaluatr")
bc_val  <- read.csv(bc_path)
bc_val  <- bc_val[bc_val$val == 1, ]

# Create the required derived variable
bc_val$log_pr <- log(bc_val$pr + 1)

# Now run validation
result_bc <- secure_model_validation(
  repo_owner      = "developer-username",
  repo_name       = "my-models",
  model_id        = "bc_cox_v1",
  github_token    = "token_provided_by_developer",
  validation_data = bc_val,
  outcome         = "rfi"
)

When the developer handles pre-processing automatically

Developers can embed transformation code directly in their model specification. In this case, you provide the raw data and evaluatr handles the rest — no additional steps are required on your side.

# No pre-processing needed — the developer's specification handles it
result_autoprepro <- secure_model_validation(
  repo_owner      = "developer-username",
  repo_name       = "my-models",
  model_id        = "bc_cox_auto_v1",
  github_token    = "token_provided_by_developer",
  validation_data = bc_val,    # raw pr provided as-is
  outcome         = "rfi"
)

The two approaches produce identical predictions; the difference is purely in who applies the transformation.

More examples: other outcome types

The examples above focus on binary outcomes and general workflow concepts. The public evaluatr demo repository also hosts models covering the other outcome types evaluatr supports. Runnable scripts for each are included with the package under system.file("extdata", package = "evaluatr"):

Script Model type Outcome
example_01_dvt_logistic.R Logistic regression Binary (DVT diagnosis)
example_02_bc_cox.R Cox proportional hazards Survival (breast cancer relapse)
example_03_bc_weibull.R Weibull AFT Survival (breast cancer relapse)
example_04_adnex_multinomial.R Multinomial logistic regression 5-category (ADNEX ovarian mass classification)

Each script uses the same public demo repository and read-only token as Example 1 above, so they can be run as-is. The survival and multinomial scripts also include independent manual verification of the predictions against a locally-fit reference model.

Minimum dataset requirements

Requirement Value
Minimum total observations 50
Minimum per subgroup (when using by) 50
Outcome variable type for eval_performance() Binary (0/1) in the current release. Survival and multinomial predictions can be computed with evaluatr, but performance metrics for these outcome types must currently be calculated independently by the evaluator; full support in eval_performance() is planned for a future release.

These thresholds exist to prevent the package from being used to obtain predictions for individual patients.

Security and data privacy

  • Your patient data never leaves your R session. No data is transmitted to GitHub or to the model developer.
  • Predictions are shuffled before being returned, so they cannot be matched back to individual patient rows.
  • Every validation run is logged by the evaluatr registry, creating an audit trail. Access tokens can be revoked by the developer at any time.
  • The package is designed exclusively for retrospective evaluation studies. It must not be used to generate predictions that inform care for individual patients.

Getting help

If you encounter problems, check the following:

  • The token provided by the developer has not expired.
  • Your dataset contains all the variable names listed in the developer’s documentation.
  • If using eval_performance(), check that the outcome variable is coded as 0/1 for binary outcomes.
  • The model_id, repo_owner, and repo_name all match exactly what the developer provided (these are case-sensitive).

See ?secure_model_validation and ?eval_performance for full argument documentation.
